sentences.text: Spicomellus holds the unique distinction of being the only known vertebrate with dermal spikes fused directly to its bone.
The genus name Spicomellus combines the Latin words for 'spike' and 'collar' to describe this unusual anatomy.
The holotype specimen consists of a single T-shaped rib with four spines fused to it, a feature unknown in any other animal.
The largest and most complete spike recovered from this animal measures 87 centimeters in length.
Estimates suggest that an adult individual of this species did not exceed three meters in total length.
This dinosaur is recognized as the oldest named definitive ankylosaur known to science.
It represents the earliest known ankylosaur in the world, though an unnamed relative from Scotland might be slightly older.
Fused handle vertebrae with ossified tendons in its tail likely indicate the presence of a defensive tail weapon.
Remains were found in the third subunit of the El Mers Group near Boulahfa, south of Boulemane in the Fès-Meknès region of Morocco.
The species Spicomellus afer was formally named and described on September 23, 2021, in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.
Lead researcher Susannah Maidment initially suspected the fossil was a forgery, but a computerized scan confirmed it was genuine.
The original description was based on a single rib fragment fused to an osteoderm.
A second specimen was later described in 2025 and is now held at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University.
Unfortunately, several bones from this species have been illegally excavated from Morocco and sold online.
Because its dorsal spines were fused to the bone rather than attached to muscle tissue like in other ankylosaurs, this trait likely made movement difficult for the animal.
The predators in its ecosystem consisted of indeterminate theropods, possibly megalosaurids.
Spicomellus is assigned to the clade Eurypoda based on the T-shaped cross section of its ribs.
Phylogenetic analysis recovered the species in an early-diverging clade within Ankylosauria outside of Ankylosauridae or Nodosauridae.
Researchers confirmed that Spicomellus is a basal ankylosaur.
The animal likely had a close relationship to the only other known ankylosaurs of the time, the genera Sarcolestes from the UK and Tianchisaurus from China.
Spicomellus lived during the Bathonian age of the Middle Jurassic in Morocco.
At that time, Morocco was part of the supercontinent Gondwana.
The species lived during the Middle Jurassic, between the Bathonian and Callovian stages, approximately 168 to 164 million years ago.
The precise time range for Spicomellus is from the Bathonian to Callovian, between 168.2 and 161.5 million years ago.
The animal inhabited what is now Africa.
Spicomellus is the second described eurypod taxon from North Africa, after Adratiklit.

The discovery of Spicomellus shows that Ankylosauria and Stegosauria coexisted for over 20 million years, implying that stegosaur extinction was caused by other unknown reasons, contradicting the traditional belief that they were displaced by ankylosaurs.
Spicomellus indicates that ankylosaurs and stegosaurs coexisted for more than 20 million years.
